summary: This experimental RFC defines an NTP extension field holding a 2-octet checksum complement. Some hardware stamps the exact send time into an outgoing NTP packet, which forces the UDP checksum to change. With the complement in the last bytes of the packet, the hardware can fix things up there instead of rewriting the UDP checksum. It stays interoperable with existing NTP implementations.

eli5.summary: A clock that writes the time on a letter as it leaves the mailbox changes the letter's weight. This adds a small balancing note at the end so the weight still adds up.

subtitle: A 2-octet balancing field that lets timestamping hardware edit an NTP packet without touching the UDP checksum.

tldr.problem: Some NTP implementations use hardware that writes the exact send time into each outgoing packet, which changes the UDP checksum and forces the hardware to rewrite it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a 28-octet NTP extension field whose last 2 octets are a Checksum Complement. The hardware sets it to cancel the change from the new timestamp, so the UDP Checksum stays correct.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol, intended for use inside an NTP client or server, not for use with authentication. The unit metadata lists RFC 9748 as updating it.

today: RFC 7821 is an Experimental RFC, not an Internet Standards Track specification, and the unit metadata lists RFC 9748 as updating it. The same mechanism for OWAMP and TWAMP is in RFC 7820.

sections.title: Why Timestamps Break Checksums
sections.content:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) lets clients synchronize their clocks to a time server by exchanging timestamped packets. To get the timestamps as accurate as possible, some implementations use a hardware timestamping engine that writes the true transmission time into the Transmit Timestamp field of each outgoing packet as it leaves.

NTP runs over UDP, so changing the payload means the UDP Checksum no longer matches. An intermediate entity that cannot fix the checksum has to set it to zero. For IPv4 that makes the receiver ignore the checksum and possibly accept corrupted packets. For IPv6 a zero checksum is not allowed except in specific cases.

The checksum can be updated incrementally, since only the timestamp changed. Even so, the RFC notes that rewriting a field in the UDP header after the timestamp, while the packet streams out in order, makes the hardware harder to build.
sections.eli5: If a machine scribbles the exact time onto a message on its way out, the message's built-in check number is now wrong. Fixing that check number at the front of the message is awkward for the machine.

sections.title: The Checksum Complement Extension Field
sections.content:
The fix is a new NTP extension field placed at the very end of the UDP payload. It is 28 octets long. It holds a field type, a length of 28 octets, a 22-octet MBZ (must be zero) padding field, and the Checksum Complement in the last 2 octets.

The MBZ bytes MUST be set to 0 and MUST be ignored by the recipient. The 28-octet length guarantees that a host parses the packet correctly whether or not it carries a Message Authentication Code (MAC). If other extension fields are present, the Checksum Complement field is always the last one, so the complement sits at (UDP Length minus 2 octets) from the start of the UDP header.

IANA allocated the extension field type 0x2005 in the NTP Extension Field Types registry.
sections.eli5: The note at the end of the message is a fixed-size slip with a few blank spaces and a tiny balancing number in the last corner.

sections.title: How the Complement Keeps the Checksum Right
sections.content:
The sender's software builds the NTP packet with the extension field and a complement of zero. The timestamping engine then replaces the timestamp with the accurate one and, in the same pass, writes a new value into the Checksum Complement. That value is chosen so that the change to the checksum caused by the new timestamp is cancelled out. The UDP Checksum already in the packet stays correct.

The receiver needs nothing special. It runs the normal UDP checksum, and the complement is simply part of the extension field it covers. The RFC's appendix works this through with the checksum of the timestamp before and after the update.

A transmitter MAY include the field, and an intermediate entity that alters such a packet MAY use the complement. The NTP layer at the receiving end SHOULD ignore the field. The software layer and the timestamping engine are two parts of a single NTP clock, and they are assumed to agree on whether the field is used.
sections.eli5: When the machine changes the time on the letter, it also changes the balancing number at the end by exactly the right amount, so the letter still weighs what the label says.

sections.title: Interoperability with Existing NTP Hosts
sections.content:
The extension adds no new requirements on receivers beyond those in RFC 7822. That RFC says a host that receives an unknown extension field SHOULD ignore it, and MAY drop the packet if policy requires. So senders that use the Checksum Complement work with receivers that ignore unknown extension fields.

Implementations that discard packets with unknown extension fields cannot interoperate with a transmitter that uses the complement. If only one side uses hardware timestamping, the field should be used only when the peer is known to accept it.
sections.eli5: Most receivers just skip a note they do not understand. A few strict ones throw the whole letter away, so you only add the note when you know the other side is fine with it.

sections.title: No Use with Authentication
sections.content: A Checksum Complement MUST NOT be used when authentication is enabled. With authentication, any entity that alters the packet must also recompute the MAC. Updating the complement would force a MAC recalculation, and the MAC would cover the complement, creating a cyclic dependency. So the UDP Checksum has to be updated directly, and the complement adds nothing.
sections.eli5: If the letter also has a tamper-proof seal, changing the balancing number would break the seal, and fixing the seal would change the number again. So with a seal, do not bother with the balancing note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is meant to be used internally in an NTP client or server, not by switches and routers between the client and the server. Unlike PTP, NTP does not need intermediate devices to change message content, so any such modification should be treated as a malicious man-in-the-middle attack.

The RFC argues the scheme does not make that attack easier. An attacker who changes a packet and its Checksum Complement is logically equivalent to one who changes a packet and its UDP Checksum. The concept is intended for unauthenticated mode only.
sections.eli5: The balancing note is for the mailbox machine only. If someone else in the middle changes your letter, that is tampering, whether they fix the note or the label.
